hasarlink_file_overview_decision.title: Making files quick to scan
hasarlink_file_overview_decision.problem: It was difficult to compare the status of different files at list level.
hasarlink_file_overview_decision.decision: Show the most important information in a summary that can be read at a glance.
hasarlink_file_overview_decision.application: I brought licence plate, insurer, and application status together in consistent list items.
hasarlink_file_overview_decision.structure: A scannable file list that helps users find the priority record quickly.

hasarlink_file_detail_decision.title: Making file status and history easy to track
hasarlink_file_detail_decision.problem: Tracking became difficult when the current stage, previous activity, and related details were disconnected.
hasarlink_file_detail_decision.decision: Bring the entire process for the selected file into one detail hierarchy.
hasarlink_file_detail_decision.application: I organised the current stage, history, party and accident information, and documents into meaningful sections.
hasarlink_file_detail_decision.structure: A file detail view connecting quick list scanning with in-depth process tracking.

hasarlink_decision_reason_label: Why did I choose this approach?

hero.title: Bringing different damage notification processes into one product flow
hero.summary: HasarLink is a mobile and web product experience that brings claims for different insurers into one shared, trackable flow.
hero.audience: Insurance service businesses and repair professionals

problem.title: Project and Problem
problem.intro: Bringing different company processes together within one product logic.

items.title: Context
items.text: Each insurer used different form fields, documents, and process steps. Users had to manage changing rules and dense information while completing the same core task.

items.title: Design problem
items.text: The goal was not simply to make long forms look better. Shared fields had to be identified, unnecessary inputs reduced, and differences retained within a clear information hierarchy.

role.title: My Role and Responsibilities
role.intro: My work covered both design and the review of technical feasibility.
role.quote: Turning a complex operation into a feasible and trackable product flow.

groups.title: Process and information architecture
groups.text: I compared company forms, identified shared and distinct fields, and structured the user flow and information architecture.

groups.title: Product experience
groups.text: I organized forms, documents, timelines, and file details for mobile and web contexts.

groups.title: Interface system
groups.text: I defined light and dark theme counterparts, reusable components, and a consistent typography structure.

groups.title: Frontend support
groups.text: I compared implemented screens with the designs and supported spacing, alignment, color, and responsive corrections when needed.

process.title: My Design Process
process.intro: The actual operation-led process used in the project.

items.title: Review
items.text: Compared existing forms and processes.

items.title: Organize
items.text: Grouped shared fields and exceptions.

items.title: Build the flow
items.text: Defined steps and information architecture.

items.title: Mobile design
items.text: Designed a single-column, step-led experience.

items.title: Web adaptation
items.text: Reframed wider space for lists and information groups.

items.title: Implementation review
items.text: Checked the coded interface and responsive behavior.

decisions.title: Core UX Decisions
decisions.intro: Decisions focused on making differences manageable without hiding them.

items.title: Bringing different insurance processes into one flow
items.problem: Different insurer requirements fragmented the same starting task.
items.decision: Bring insurance company and application type choices into a shared start through controlled steps.
items.application: Users first select the relevant insurer, then specify which party's coverage the claim is opened under.
items.structure: A shared starting flow that manages insurer-specific requirements.

items.title: Breaking the long form into steps while preserving user control
items.problem: Dense information fields, especially on mobile, made it difficult to track the current stage and missing details.
items.decision: Users needed to focus only on the current stage and review their answers before continuing.
items.application: I divided victim, driver, and vehicle information into steps, presented documents in separate upload cards, and added a summary where choices can be reviewed and edited before continuing.
items.structure: A form experience combining data entry, document upload, and user review in one stepped flow.

items.title: Document reading with form review
items.problem: Document data had to be entered again.
items.decision: Connect document reading to the form while preserving user control.
items.application: Suggested data appeared in editable fields and was not treated as a final result.
items.structure: A flow combining automation suggestions with user verification.

items.title: Sectioning file details
items.problem: Different information types crowded one view.
items.application: File, claimant, document, and repair details were grouped.

items.title: Making file status and history easy to track
items.problem: Operational tracking became difficult when current status, past activity, and related details were presented separately.
items.decision: Users needed to scan files quickly before drilling into the record they needed.
items.application: I summarized licence plate, insurer, and application status in the list. The detail view brings together the current stage, history, party information, accident details, and documents in meaningful sections.
items.structure: A two-level file architecture connecting quick list scanning with detailed process tracking.

items.title: Draft and correction flows
items.problem: Incomplete or rejected files sat outside the main process.
items.decision: Treat continuation and correction as core states.
items.application: Saving drafts and returning to missing fields became part of the flow.
items.structure: A process covering interruptions and rework.

collaboration.title: Working with the Development Team
collaboration.intro: It was not enough for the designs to look correct only in Figma.
collaboration.text: My role was not to build the entire frontend, but to review implementation quality against design decisions and support interface work when needed.
items: Spacing, sizing, alignment, and color review
Interface adjustments in code when needed

learnings.title: What I Learned
learnings.intro: The project showed the importance of considering dense operational information across design and implementation.
learnings.quote: A design system makes decisions consistent, not just screens.

items.title: Simplifying does not mean deleting information.
items.text: Keeping necessary detail while presenting it at the right time and in the right group mattered more.

items.title: Responsive design reprioritizes information.
items.text: Instead of scaling one hierarchy, I rebuilt it for mobile and web contexts.

items.title: Automation should not replace user control.
items.text: Document-reading suggestions remained editable and verifiable.

items.title: Good design must keep working when coded.
items.text: Variable data, responsive behavior, and component reuse became part of implementation review.

articles_intro: Technical notes, walkthroughs, and learning logs on UX Design, frontend development, React, and Next.js.
career_text: I began my career as a social services graduate, and my interest in the world of software led me toward frontend development. Through the Front-End training I received at Acunmedya Akademi, I built a strong foundation in technologies such as HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React, and Next.js. Over time, I realized that creating strong digital products is not only about writing code, but also about structuring the user experience in the right way, which led me to move into the field of UI/UX design. By completing the Google UX Design program on Coursera, I strengthened my design perspective and improved myself in areas such as user-centered thinking, wireframing, prototyping, and interface design.
projects_teamwork_text: I have taken an active role in UI/UX design processes for the digital products I worked on. I created interface designs by evaluating user needs, business goals, and product flows together. My frontend knowledge and the development support I provided when needed helped me evaluate design decisions from a technical feasibility perspective. Experiencing the connection between design and development firsthand enabled me to create more feasible, consistent, and user-centered products. Collaborating across disciplines strengthened both my design skills and my product development perspective.
learning_sharing_text: Each project has helped me progress in my field of expertise and contributed to my continuous growth. The knowledge I have gained, especially in user experience, interface design, and product development processes, has deepened my professional perspective even further. I value sharing the design and development approaches I have learned not only in my own work processes, but also through the articles I write on Medium in order to benefit others. With a mindset that is always learning, researching, and producing, I continue to improve myself every day.
future_vision_text: Throughout my career journey, I focus on creating stronger digital products by combining my knowledge of design and development. As I continue to deepen my expertise in UI/UX design, I care about supporting design decisions with feasible and sustainable solutions thanks to my technical background. My goal is to create products that are not only visually strong, but also functional, accessible, and capable of building a real connection with users. With my disciplined work ethic and openness to learning, I aim to continue taking part in projects that create value on both the design and development sides in the future.
entertainment_web_app_text: Entertainment Web App is a platform where users can discover movies and TV series and add them to their personal favorites list. The project was rebuilt with Next.js, and Supabase was integrated for user authentication and personalized data management. Each user can only view their own bookmarked content. All data is dynamically fetched from the Supabase database, with global state managed via useContext and routing handled through the Next.js App Router. Designed with a mobile-first approach, the app offers a clean and modern user experience.
blog_page_text: In this project I use hash routing structure with React to manage application navigation and useContext for theme switching. I manage data using API with POST, PUT, and DELETE operations. Security is ensured with username and password validation, allowing only logged-in users to edit and delete posts. I created the design myself to offer a user-friendly and modern interface. The project successfully integrated API, providing a secure and functional experience.
rest_countries_text: This project is a React application that dynamically displays information about world countries. Users can search between countries, filter by regions, and find the countries they are looking for. Detailed basic and additional information is provided for each country. Dark mode support personalizes the user experience, and the theme preference is stored in local storage. With hash-based routing and responsive design, the application offers a user-friendly experience on all devices.
dev_jobs_text: DevJobs Web App is a React application developed as a group project with Gökdeniz Keleş at Acunmedya Akademi, which allows users to filter and view developer job listings. Dynamic data management and filtering features allow job listings to be easily searched and sorted. With theme management, users can switch between dark and light modes, and preferences are saved in local storage. Mobile-first design and flexible structures ensure a user-friendly experience on all screen sizes. Job listings can be clicked to view detailed cards with information.
dictionary_web_app_text: The Dictionary App is a React application that allows users to easily access word meanings, pronunciations, synonyms, and example sentences. Word data is dynamically fetched via API, allowing users to quickly find the words they are looking for. With theme management, users can switch between light and dark modes, and preferences are stored in local storage. The app offers three different font options to enrich the user experience. The application is made faster and more sustainable due to React's modular structure.
markdown_editor_text: Markdown Editor is a React application that instantly converts users' Markdown writings into previews. Users can create new files, update and delete existing ones, and changes are saved with localStorage. With theme management, users can switch between light and dark modes. The responsive design ensures a mobile-first experience that is compatible with all devices. File operations are dynamically and interactively designed to improve the user experience.
frontend_quiz_text: Frontend Quiz App is an interactive quiz application that offers 10-question tests in HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Accessibility categories. Users choose one of these four categories and start answering questions. Correct and incorrect answers are visually shown on the results screen, and the correct answer is immediately displayed when the user provides an incorrect answer. The application provides feedback to the user before moving between questions, making the learning process more interactive. Theme management allows users to switch between light and dark modes, and theme preferences are saved in localStorage.
memory_game_text: Memory Game is a fun game application where players match cards to progress. The cards are shuffled at the start, and each new game presents a different arrangement. Feedback is given when the selected cards match, and the game ends when all the cards are matched. The game also features a timer and move counter. With mobile-first design, the game offers a compatible experience on all devices.
product_list_with_card_text: In this project, users can add products to their cart, change quantities, and see the total amount in real-time. When a product is added to the cart, the quantity automatically increases, and the total amount is recalculated in real-time. With mobile-first design, the application offers a compatible experience on both desktop and mobile devices.
post_list_text: In this project, I enabled users to view different posts and dynamically explore the comments of each post. Data is fetched from three different API endpoints, providing dynamic content for post lists, post details, and post comments. I managed data using useState and prop drilling. The application is optimized for both desktop and mobile devices with modern CSS techniques and a responsive design.
landing_page_text: In this project, I collaborated with Hilal Baran and Atakan Arıkan on a Git-based team project. Using Git version control systems, we developed the project in an organized and efficient way. We designed a landing page with HTML and CSS, featuring Careers, Blog, Pricing, Help & Support, About, and Contact Us sections. By experiencing the importance of teamwork, we reinforced our frontend skills.
kanban_text: During the Acunmedya Academy bootcamp, we developed the Kanban Task Management Web App with İrem Çoban and Mehmet Akif Küçükyılmaz. Users can create boards and columns, add, edit, move, and delete tasks. All data is stored in localStorage to prevent data loss. With a responsive design and dark mode support, the user experience was improved. React state management was effectively used to create a dynamic structure, and React Hot Toast was integrated for real-time notifications. Soon, we plan to enhance interaction by adding a drag-and-drop feature using the @dnd-kit library.
product_feedback_text: During the Acunmedya Academy bootcamp, our team successfully completed the Product Feedback App project. We effectively utilized the GIT version control system for collaboration. Users can reply to comments, add new ones, edit, and delete them. We categorized comments by tags, allowing users to filter them, and created a sorting menu to display the most/least liked or commented feedback. A roadmap page was developed to track the status of comments. We implemented hash routing for navigation and used React Hot Toast for real-time notifications. All data is stored in localStorage to prevent data loss. In the future, we plan to enhance the user experience by integrating an authentication system.
xox_game: This project is a React application that reimagines the classic Tic Tac Toe game with a modern interface and user authentication. Users are greeted with a game selection screen and prompted to log in before choosing their mark (X or O). The game tracks wins, losses, and ties, updating the score accordingly. Scores are preserved when a new round starts. With dark mode support and a responsive design, the game offers a seamless experience across all devices. Player preferences are stored using local storage, and global state management is handled via the Context API. This user-friendly design, built through strong team collaboration, demonstrates effective use of the React ecosystem.

hero.title: One Mobile Experience, Before and After an Accident
hero.summary1: Zayfix QRakter is a mobile vehicle and community app that lets users prepare emergency information, manage documents, and create an Individual or Shared digital accident report.
hero.summary2: Its five-step report flow brings driver and vehicle details, impact points, photos, location, scenario drawing, review, and signatures into one controlled process. The on-the-move and gloved usage conditions of motorcyclists and couriers shaped the visibility of critical actions.
hero.platform: Mobile · Android app / mobile web access on iOS
hero.target: Vehicle users, especially motorcyclists and couriers

problem.title: Project and Problem
problem.intro: Managing prepared information, intensive accident-time data entry, and post-accident follow-up in one mobile system.

items.title: Product context
items.text: Zayfix QRakter treats an accident as a lifecycle. Users prepare profile, health, vehicle, and document data; create a QR Emergency Card and pair a physical QR code; start an Individual or Shared report; and track records in My Reports.

items.title: Design problem
items.text: The report requires controlled completion of driver, vehicle, insurance, location, photo, impact, statement, witness, scenario, and signature data. Progress and missing information had to remain clear under stressful, mobile, or gloved use.

items.title: Approach
items.text: Structure the lifecycle around before, during, and after an accident; divide complex flows into steps and prioritise critical actions for real usage conditions.

role.title: My Role and Contributions
role.intro: I designed every mobile interface, from onboarding, profiles, documents, and the QR Emergency Card to the five-step report, clubs, community, and rewards. I provided focused frontend support in code where needed to preserve design fidelity.

items.title: Product flows and complete interface design
items.text: I designed the entire mobile experience across preparation, reporting, follow-up, community, and rewards.

items.title: Accident-report information architecture
items.text: I divided the intensive report into five stages and designed Individual and Shared participation and pre-signature checks.

items.title: Forms and data management
items.text: I connected categories, filters, validation, automated entry, and user verification across profiles, documents, and reports.

items.title: Frontend support
items.text: I supported spacing, alignment, input consistency, filtering, accordions, validation, and guidance boxes directly in code.

process.title: My Design Process
process.intro: An iterative process combining real usage conditions, product flows, and technical feasibility.

items.title: Understanding the product lifecycle
items.text: I reviewed the complete journey from prepared information to accident reporting and follow-up.

items.title: Setting information priorities
items.text: I grouped emergency, profile, document, QR, report, and support actions by the moment of need.

items.title: Breaking complexity into steps
items.text: I separated driver, vehicle, insurance, evidence, scenario, and signature data into controlled stages.

items.title: Designing roles and states
items.text: I treated Individual and Shared reports, user roles, and draft, active, and completed states as distinct experiences.

items.title: Development and iteration
items.text: I reviewed flows with developers, revised screens from feedback, and supported design fidelity in code.

decisions.title: Core UX Decisions
decisions.intro: Turning real usage problems into visible, accessible, and feasible product decisions.

items.title: Turning a complex accident report into a controlled step-by-step flow
items.problem: The report required extensive driver, vehicle, insurance, impact, evidence, scenario, and signature data.
items.reason: Under stress, users should focus only on the current information group.
items.application: I designed five stages: Driver and Vehicle Details, Accident Details and Evidence, Accident Scenario, Review, and Signature. Individual reports work on one device; Shared reports let each party contribute from their own device.
items.result: A report with visible progress and correction before signing.

items.title: Reusing prepared information in the QR card and report
items.problem: Re-entering identity, health, vehicle, and insurance data during an accident increased effort and risk.
items.reason: Information should be prepared before an incident and reused in critical flows.
items.application: I categorised profile data, linked it to the QR Emergency Card and report, designed role-based QR privacy, physical QR pairing, and downloadable templates.
items.result: A connected preparation system that avoids starting from zero at a critical moment.

items.title: Making participation requirements and outcome states clear in the Prize Wheel
items.problem: The experience became unclear when users could not understand under which conditions they could spin the wheel, why missing profile information blocked participation, or what they should do after receiving a result.
items.reason: Showing only the reward result was not enough. The participation requirement, current state and next action also needed to remain clear.
items.application: In addition to the default Prize Wheel screen, I designed a blocked state that prevents participation when required profile information is missing and clearly shows which fields need to be completed. For an unsuccessful result, I also made the next spin availability and the user's next action visible.
items.result: A state-based reward experience that separates the default, blocked and result states while clearly showing users what they can do at each stage.

items.title: Turning home into a hub for accident and vehicle actions
items.problem: Small emergency controls and scattered vehicle actions slowed access.
items.reason: Home needed to support the before, during, and after-accident lifecycle.
items.application: I enlarged SOS and emergency actions and prioritised the QR card, profile, documents, New Report, My Reports, and Accident Support.
items.result: One fast starting point for critical vehicle and accident actions.

items.title: Making profiles and reports trackable by status
items.problem: Long profiles and undifferentiated report histories obscured missing and unfinished work.
items.reason: Users needed to see their current state and next action.
items.application: I grouped profiles in accordions and separated reports into Draft, Active, and Completed states with useful card summaries.
items.result: Status-based tracking for personal preparation and accident records.

items.title: Adapting the club experience to the user's role
items.problem: Showing the same actions to club owners and regular members mixed management permissions with standard membership tasks.
items.reason: Users should only see actions relevant to their role, while the club's core information should remain consistent for both roles.
items.application: For club owners, I provided management actions such as creating announcements, managing membership requests, organizing giveaways, editing club information and submitting deletion requests. For regular users, I prioritized announcements, club information and the action to join the club.
items.result: A role-based club experience that keeps the same club structure while clearly separating administrator and member responsibilities.

collaboration.title: Working with the Development Team
collaboration.intro: The implemented product needed to preserve the flows and behaviours defined in Figma.
collaboration.text: I reviewed data-heavy, role-sensitive areas such as home, profile, QR card, reports, clubs, and community directly with the developers, including how parties join Individual and Shared reports.
items: Correcting spacing, alignment, and sizing in code
Maintaining input consistency, filters, and validation
Coding the profile accordion and guidance boxes
collaboration.outro: I did not build the entire frontend; I protected design decisions and provided direct UI/frontend support where needed.

learnings.title: What I Learned
learnings.intro: The project showed the importance of considering real usage conditions across design and implementation.

items.title: Complex tasks should not be forced onto one screen
items.text: Breaking the report into meaningful steps improved focus and visibility of missing information.

items.title: Prepared data reduces pressure at a critical moment
items.text: Reusing profile, health, vehicle, and insurance data reduced repeat entry.

items.title: Automation must not replace user control
items.text: Policy analysis accelerated entry, while explicit official-document verification protected reliability.

items.title: Touch targets must reflect usage conditions
items.text: Critical actions had to work with thick motorcycle gloves.

lifecycle.title: Product Flow from Before to After an Accident
lifecycle.intro: A connected structure from preparing reusable information to completing the report and reaching post-accident services.

items.title: Prepare information in advance
items.text: Users prepare profile, health, vehicle, insurance, and document details and create a QR Emergency Card. The same data can be reused in the card and report.

items.title: Manage the accident and report
items.text: Users reach SOS, emergency services, or support and start an Individual or Shared report. Five steps control party, vehicle, evidence, scenario, signature, and verification data.

items.title: Track records and reach services
items.text: Reports can be previewed, downloaded, and shared. Draft, active, and completed records remain trackable alongside towing, repair, and insurer access.
